kits.familyName: What is really blocking the deadline
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You are responsible for {deliverable|the}, which is due at 3 p.m. today.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are responsible for {deliverable|the}, due at 3 p.m.
pressure: {coworker3} says {lead|the} hates late work and you need to finish no matter what.
detail: The rest of the team is busy with their own work.
It has been a quiet afternoon so far.

tiers.1: A safety step is never traded for speed.
tiers.2: Wrong work has to be stopped before it reaches anyone.
tiers.3: You need to know which job matters most before planning your time.
tiers.4: The job cannot be finished correctly without what is missing.
tiers.5: New ideas can wait until urgent problems are handled.

fact: Finishing by 3 p.m. would mean skipping the safety check that {lead|the} requires at the end.
issues.action: Keep the safety check and let {lead|the} know the work will be late.
issues.brief: keep the safety check and warn {lead|the} it will be late
issues.reason: A late delivery is a smaller problem than an unsafe one. Telling the lead early lets them adjust plans.
issues.lesson: When a deadline and a safety step collide, keep the safety step and communicate the delay.

shortcut.text: Skip the safety check this once so {deliverable|the} is on time.
shortcut.brief: skip the safety check this once
shortcut.why: Skipping a required safety check puts people at risk. Being on time does not make that acceptable.
shortcut.mis: Meeting a deadline justifies skipping a step once.

fact: While reviewing, you find a mistake in the part of the job you already completed.
issues.short: the mistake in the finished part
issues.action: Correct the mistake, or report it to {lead|the}, before anything is delivered.
issues.brief: correct or report the mistake before delivery
issues.reason: Delivering work you know is wrong passes the problem to the people relying on it. Stopping it now is cheaper than fixing it later.
issues.lesson: Stop known errors before work is delivered, even if it costs time.

shortcut.text: Deliver {deliverable|the} on time and fix the mistake in the next version.
shortcut.brief: deliver on time and fix it next time
shortcut.why: Sending work you know is wrong spreads the error to everyone who uses it.
shortcut.mis: On time matters more than correct.

fact: {Lead|the} also asked you to finish a second job by 3 p.m., and there is not time for both.
clear: {Lead|the} told you this morning that the second job can wait until tomorrow.
issues.done: the lead already said which job comes first
issues.action: Explain the conflict to {lead|the} and ask which job should come first.
issues.reason: Only the lead can decide which deadline matters more. Raising the conflict early gives them time to choose or find help.
issues.lesson: When deadlines overlap, raise the conflict and let the person in charge set the priority.

shortcut.text: Split your time between both jobs and hope both get done.
shortcut.brief: split your time between both jobs
shortcut.why: Without a priority you may finish neither. The lead needs to decide which job matters more.
shortcut.mis: Doing a little of everything is the safest plan.

fact: A measurement you need from {coworker} has not arrived yet.
clear: {coworker} sent the measurement you needed an hour ago.
issues.action: Contact {coworker} to get the measurement, and keep working on other parts meanwhile.
issues.reason: The job depends on that number. Asking for it directly is fast, and working on other parts meanwhile saves time.
issues.lesson: Identify the missing information the job depends on and go get it.

shortcut.text: Estimate the measurement from a similar past job and keep going.
shortcut.brief: estimate the measurement from an old job
shortcut.why: A guessed number can make the whole job wrong. Getting the real figure is quick compared with redoing work.
shortcut.mis: A reasonable guess is as good as the real number.

fact: The {supply.plural} the job needs are out of stock.
clear: A delivery of {supply.plural} arrived this morning.
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} about an approved substitute and explain how it affects the deadline.
issues.reason: The lead knows which substitutes meet the job's requirements. Asking also warns them about the possible delay.
issues.lesson: When a resource runs out, check approved alternatives and say how it affects the schedule.

shortcut.text: Use whatever similar supply is on the shelf without asking anyone.
shortcut.brief: use a similar supply without asking
shortcut.why: An unapproved substitute may not meet the job's requirements, and nobody will know it was changed.
shortcut.mis: If it looks the same, it works the same.

fact: You notice a way the job could be done faster next time.
issues.action: Write the idea down and share it once today's job is delivered.
issues.brief: note the idea for after the deadline
issues.reason: The idea is worth keeping, but trying a new method under a deadline adds risk. Noting it protects both the deadline and the idea.
issues.lesson: Capture improvement ideas without letting them derail urgent work.

shortcut.text: Switch to the new method right now to save time.
shortcut.why: Changing methods halfway through a deadline job risks new mistakes.
shortcut.mis: A faster idea should always be used immediately.

proceed.text: Keep working on {deliverable|the} so it is ready by 3 p.m.
proceed.why: Nothing in the situation blocks the work, so the best move is to keep going and finish on time.
proceed.lesson: When the information, resources and priorities are in place, focus on finishing the work.

generic.text: Stop working and wait for someone to notice there is a problem.
generic.why: Waiting silently lets the deadline pass without anyone being able to help.
generic.mis: Problems get solved if you wait.

generic.text: Complain about the deadline to {coworker2} but keep it from {lead|the}.
generic.why: Venting to a coworker changes nothing. The lead needs to hear about problems to help.
generic.mis: Telling someone is the same as telling the right person.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to recheck the whole job before you continue.
overcaution.why: Nothing in the situation calls for a full recheck. Asking for one delays work that is ready to continue.
overcaution.mis: Asking for extra checks is always the responsible choice.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, responsible for {deliverable|the} due at 3 p.m.

steps.text: Get an approved substitute for the {supply}
Check the finished work before handing it in

rel: You need to know the requirements before doing the work.
Reviewing the requirements shows what is missing.
The requirements tell you what a substitute must match.
The work depends on the measurement.
You need to know which job to work on first.
The work cannot be done without the supplies.
You can only check work once it is done.
process.lesson: Know the requirements, clear what blocks the work, do it, then check it.

title: Update on {deliverable|the}
intro: You are about to send {lead|the} this status update. Check it first.
doc.lesson: A status update should be accurate, early and honest about what is at risk.

lines.text: Here is an update on {deliverable|the}, which is due at 3 p.m.
lines.fine: States what the update is about and the deadline.

lines.text: The first half is finished and I checked it against the job requirements.
lines.fine: Reports progress and that it was checked.

bad.text: The first half is finished; I did not check it, but it should be fine.
bad.why: Unchecked work reported as done hides a risk. Check it or say clearly that it has not been checked.

lines.text: I am waiting on a measurement from {coworker}, which I requested at 10 a.m.
lines.fine: Names exactly what is missing and what was done about it.

bad.text: The measurement never arrived, so I used my best guess for now.
bad.why: A guessed number can make the job wrong. The real measurement should be obtained, or the guess flagged as a risk.

lines.text: I will keep the final safety check, even if it takes extra time.

bad.text: To stay on time, I will skip the final safety check.
bad.why: A deadline never justifies skipping a required safety check.

lines.text: You also asked me to finish the second job by 3 p.m.
Could you tell me which job should come first?
lines.fine: Asks the person in charge to set the priority.

bad.text: I will work on both jobs at once until 3 p.m.
bad.why: Both jobs are due at the same time. Splitting effort risks finishing neither; the lead should choose which comes first.

lines.text: I will send another update at noon.
lines.fine: Promises the next update before the deadline.

bad.text: I will let you know after 3 p.m. if anything went wrong.
bad.why: Reporting after the deadline removes the lead's chance to help. Problems should be raised before the deadline.

review.notes: Mirrors the five obstacle types (missing information, conflicting priorities, safety, resources, incorrect work). Missing information and missing supplies share a tier and are exclusive because their order is a matter of judgment.

kits.familyName: Finding the cause of recurring errors
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. For weeks, {record|the} has kept coming back with errors, and {lead|the} asked you to help fix it.
At {workplace|the}, errors keep showing up in {record|the}. {Lead|the} asked you, {role|a}, to help solve the problem.
pressure: {coworker3} says the team just needs to act fast and stop talking about it.
detail: The errors are not dangerous, but they waste time.
It is a busy week at {workplace|the}.

tiers.1: Without evidence about the errors, every fix is a guess.
tiers.2: Checking whether the last fix worked comes before adding another.
tiers.3: Blame without evidence can be unfair and can hide the real cause.
tiers.4: Extra checking treats the symptom, so it comes after understanding the cause.

fact: Nobody has written down when or where the errors happen.
clear: {coworker} has logged every error, with the time and shift, for the past two weeks.
issues.done: the errors were already logged for two weeks
issues.short: the lack of any record of the errors
issues.action: Start logging when and where each error happens before choosing a fix.
issues.brief: start logging when and where errors happen
issues.reason: Without a record, any fix is a guess. A short log shows patterns that point to the real cause.
issues.lesson: Collect evidence about a problem before deciding how to fix it.

shortcut.text: Pick the fix most coworkers prefer, since there is no data anyway.
shortcut.why: Popularity is not evidence. A fix chosen without data may miss the cause entirely.
shortcut.mis: When there is no data, opinion is good enough.

fact: {coworker}'s log shows nearly every error happens during the evening shift.
issues.action: Find out what is different about the evening shift before changing anything.
issues.brief: find out what is different about evenings
issues.reason: The pattern points to something about the evening shift, such as training, staffing or equipment. Targeting that difference addresses the cause.
issues.lesson: Let patterns in the evidence point you toward the cause.

shortcut.text: Retrain staff on every shift, just to be safe.
shortcut.why: The evidence points to one shift. Retraining everyone spends effort where there is no problem.
shortcut.mis: Treating everyone the same is the fairest fix, whatever the data show.

fact: A new checklist was introduced last week, but nobody has checked whether it reduced the errors.
clear: You compared the records: errors dropped by half after last week's checklist.
issues.done: you already confirmed the checklist cut errors in half
issues.short: the unchecked effect of last week's fix
issues.action: Compare errors before and after last week's checklist to see whether it helped.
issues.brief: check whether last week's checklist helped
issues.reason: Knowing whether the first fix worked tells you whether to keep it, adjust it or try something else.
issues.lesson: After putting a fix in place, check whether it actually worked.

shortcut.text: Assume the checklist worked, since nobody has complained this week.
shortcut.why: A quiet week is not evidence. The records show whether errors actually went down.
shortcut.mis: No complaints means the problem is solved.

fact: {coworker2} says the newest employee must be careless and should get a warning.
issues.short: the blame aimed at the newest employee
issues.action: Point out that the records should show the cause before anyone is blamed.
issues.brief: ask for evidence before blaming anyone
issues.reason: Blaming a person without evidence can be unfair and can hide a cause in the process itself.
issues.lesson: Look at the evidence before blaming a person for a problem.

shortcut.text: Agree that the new employee should be warned to be more careful.
shortcut.brief: agree to warn the new employee
shortcut.why: There is no evidence the new employee causes the errors. A warning may be unfair and leave the real cause in place.
shortcut.mis: The newest person is usually the cause of new problems.

fact: {coworker3} proposes having a second person double-check every {record}.
issues.action: Compare the double-check idea with fixes that would remove the cause of the errors.
issues.brief: weigh the double-check against fixing the cause
issues.reason: Double-checking catches errors but adds work forever. A fix that removes the cause may cost less over time.
issues.lesson: Prefer solutions that remove a problem's cause over ones that only catch its symptoms.

shortcut.text: Support the double-check right away, since it is sure to catch errors.
shortcut.why: Catching errors is not the same as preventing them. The extra work never ends if the cause stays.
shortcut.mis: More checking is the best way to stop mistakes.

proceed.text: Use the logged evidence to choose a fix aimed at the cause, then track the results.
proceed.why: The evidence is in place and the earlier fix has been measured, so the next step is a targeted fix and follow-up.
proceed.lesson: When the evidence is in, act on the cause it points to and keep measuring.

generic.text: Tell {lead|the} the errors are just bad luck and will stop on their own.
generic.why: Errors that keep happening for weeks have a cause. Calling them luck leaves the problem in place.

generic.text: Fix each error yourself as it comes in, so nobody else is bothered.
generic.why: Fixing each case hides the problem and adds to your workload. The cause stays in place.
generic.mis: Fixing each case is the same as solving the problem.

overcaution.text: Collect another month of data before making any recommendation.
overcaution.why: There is already enough evidence to act. Waiting a month lets the errors continue.
overcaution.mis: More data is always better than acting.

setup: {Lead|the} asked you to help solve a recurring problem with {record|the} at {workplace|the}.

steps.text: Record the time and shift of each mistake
Look for a pattern in those records
Measure what last week's checklist changed
Try a fix aimed at the likely cause
Count mistakes again after the fix

rel: You need logged errors before you can find a pattern.
The pattern tells you what the fix should target.
Knowing whether the earlier fix worked shapes the next one.
You can only measure a fix after it is in place.
process.lesson: Gather evidence, find the pattern, fix the cause, then measure the result.

nodata: So far, nobody has kept any record of the mistakes.
followup: A change made a few days ago has never been evaluated.

title: Problem analysis: errors in {record|the}
intro: {Lead|the} asked you to review this draft analysis before it goes to the team.
doc.lesson: A good problem analysis separates evidence from assumptions and aims the fix at the cause.

lines.text: Problem: errors in {record|the} have come back every week for a month.
lines.fine: A clear description of the problem and how long it has lasted.

lines.text: Evidence: the two-week log shows 18 of 20 errors happened on the evening shift.
Likely cause: the evening shift uses an older version of the form.
lines.fine: A cause that fits the evidence.

bad.text: Likely cause: the newest employee is careless.
bad.why: Nothing in the evidence points to one person. The errors cluster on a shift, which suggests a process or tool cause.

lines.text: Proposed fix: replace the old forms on the evening shift.
lines.fine: The fix targets the likely cause.

bad.text: Proposed fix: have a second person recheck every form on every shift.
bad.why: The analysis names an old form as the cause, but this fix only catches errors after they happen and adds work on every shift.

lines.text: Follow-up: compare error counts for two weeks after the change.
lines.fine: Plans to measure whether the fix worked.

bad.text: Follow-up: none needed, since the fix will obviously work.
bad.why: Without follow-up, no one will know whether the fix worked.

lines.text: Owner: {coworker} will track the counts and report to {lead|the}.
Data source: error log kept by {coworker}.
lines.fine: Names the source of the evidence.

bad.text: Data source: what people in the break room have been saying.
bad.why: Break-room talk is not reliable evidence. The analysis needs recorded data.

review.notes: Root-cause kit. Ambiguous pairings (no data vs follow-up, pattern vs follow-up) are exclusive.
